context_label: Completely resected melanoma with lymph-node involvement or metastatic disease; the team confirms the stage III or resected stage IV indication. Uveal melanoma is excluded from this adjuvant pathway.
purpose: Nivolumab helps immune cells act against melanoma. After complete surgery, its aim is to lower the risk of recurrence; this does not guarantee that melanoma will not return.
schedule_summary: Nivolumab every 4 weeks. Adjuvant treatment continues for up to 12 months, subject to safety review.

timeline_note: This calendar shows the pattern. Your team supplies actual dates, prescribed doses and any hold or restart instructions.
safety_note: The prescribed dose, treatment decision and local urgent-contact plan take priority. Call 112 or 999 for severe breathing difficulty, severe chest pain, collapse, a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow your oncology unit’s written urgent-contact plan for other new or worsening symptoms; do not wait for the next appointment.
teachback: Can you explain your treatment setting, medicine schedule, next tests, the symptoms that need urgent advice and the number you would call?
consent_support: Discuss the exact diagnosis, treatment intent, expected benefits and uncertainty, suitable alternatives, the regimen-specific risks and monitoring, fertility and pregnancy precautions, and practical burdens. Confirm the treatment phase and route. This guide supports the conversation and does not replace individual consent.
urgent_extra: Immunotherapy can cause inflammation in healthy organs during treatment or after it stops. Contact the oncology team promptly for new diarrhoea, blood in stools, cough or breathlessness, yellow skin or eyes, severe headache, vision changes, marked thirst, unusual weakness or a spreading rash. Tell any clinician that you are receiving or have received immunotherapy.

agents.name: Nivolumab
agents.explanation: Nivolumab blocks the PD-1 checkpoint that restrains T cells. The resulting immune activity may control melanoma but can also inflame normal organs. Side effects may first appear after the final dose.
agents.watch: Carry your immunotherapy alert card and report new symptoms early, including after treatment ends.
risks: Immune inflammation of bowel, lungs, liver or kidneys
Thyroid, pituitary, adrenal and glucose problems
Skin reactions and rare severe skin injury
Rare heart, muscle, neurological and eye inflammation
Some immune effects need long-term treatment

passport_visit_note: Record the actual date, treatment received, any hold, important symptom and the next check. A review visit is not automatically a medicine dose or a completed cycle.
anatomy_note: The established anatomical illustration links body areas to the full regimen-specific descriptions. A body location helps explain possible effects; it does not diagnose the cause of a symptom or indicate its frequency.
anatomy: New severe headache, visual change, unusual tiredness, dizziness, thirst or frequent urination may signal immune effects and needs prompt advice.
New cough or breathlessness may reflect lung inflammation or another serious cause. Call promptly; severe breathing difficulty is an emergency.
Chest pain, palpitations, marked muscle weakness or swallowing difficulty can be serious immune effects. Seek urgent assessment.
Inflammation may first show in blood tests. Report yellow eyes or skin, dark urine, unusual itching or upper-abdominal pain.
Kidney inflammation may be detected on blood tests. Report reduced urine, swelling, blood in urine or a marked change from normal.
Report increased stool frequency, diarrhoea, blood or mucus, or abdominal pain early. Severe pain, black stools or dehydration needs urgent help.
Report rash or itching early. Blistering, peeling, mouth or genital sores, or rash with fever needs urgent assessment.
New tingling, weakness, unsteadiness, facial change or trouble swallowing needs prompt review. Sudden weakness or speech difficulty is an emergency.

phases.label: Adjuvant treatment after surgery
phases.detail: Nivolumab is given as 480 mg by IV infusion over 60 minutes OR 1200 mg by subcutaneous injection over 3–5 minutes, on Day 1 every 4 weeks. Allow extra time for assessment, preparation and observation. The team selects one formulation. A subcutaneous injection is given into the thigh or abdomen, alternating sites and avoiding damaged skin, scars or moles. IV and subcutaneous doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Adjuvant treatment continues for up to 12 months, subject to safety review.

chronology_notes.title: Your schedule
chronology_notes.text: Nivolumab every 4 weeks. Adjuvant treatment continues for up to 12 months, subject to safety review.

chronology_notes.title: Held or missed treatment
chronology_notes.text: If a visit is missed or treatment is held, contact the unit for a new plan. Do not count a missed appointment as a dose received. An interval change, operation or new phase does not erase earlier immune toxicity or a permanent-stop decision.

chronology_notes.title: Tests between visits
chronology_notes.text: Blood count, kidney/liver tests and glucose before every 4-week cycle. Thyroid function is checked before each cycle and when clinically indicated. Cortisol and other tests are added when clinically indicated. Report new symptoms at every visit and between visits; normal blood results do not rule out immune toxicity.

chronology_notes.title: Safety decisions
chronology_notes.text: Routine dose reductions are not recommended for these immunotherapies. The clinician may hold or stop treatment and treat the immune effect.

chronology_notes.title: Changing the interval
chronology_notes.text: If changing from two-weekly to four-weekly nivolumab, the first four-weekly dose is two weeks after the last two-weekly dose. For the reverse change, the first two-weekly dose is four weeks after the last four-weekly dose. The team confirms the formulation and dates.

administration_text: Nivolumab is given as 480 mg by IV infusion over 60 minutes OR 1200 mg by subcutaneous injection over 3–5 minutes, on Day 1 every 4 weeks. Allow extra time for assessment, preparation and observation. The team selects one formulation. A subcutaneous injection is given into the thigh or abdomen, alternating sites and avoiding damaged skin, scars or moles. IV and subcutaneous doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram.
monitoring_summary: Blood count, kidney and liver tests, glucose and thyroid tests; review autoimmune conditions, transplants, previous immune reactions and all current medicines. BRAF tumour status is checked for the advanced or adjuvant melanoma indication. Blood count, kidney/liver tests and glucose before every 4-week cycle. Thyroid function is checked before each cycle and when clinically indicated. Cortisol and other tests are added when clinically indicated. Report new symptoms at every visit and between visits; normal blood results do not rule out immune toxicity. Continue immune-toxicity monitoring for at least five months after the last dose, and longer when advised. Keep any prescribed steroid taper, hormone replacement and specialist follow-up. Scans follow your individual disease plan.

support.title: An individual symptom plan
support.text: Ask which anti-sickness or other symptom medicines are prescribed, when to take them and when to call if they do not help. Do not start a borrowed medicine or alter treatment to manage a side effect yourself.

support.title: Your urgent contacts
support.text: Keep your actual oncology, out-of-hours and pharmacy contacts on the wallet card. Example numbers on a template must be replaced before you use it.

support.title: Pregnancy and fertility precautions
support.text: Discuss fertility before starting. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 5 months after the last dose. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy. Discuss breastfeeding restrictions with the team before treatment; do not breastfeed without their advice. Do not stop prescribed steroids or hormone replacement yourself.

support.title: Eating, activity and practical help
support.text: Let the team know if cramps, altered taste or poor appetite make eating or moving difficult. Ask for practical food and activity advice that fits your symptoms and any other illness.

support.title: Steroids and hormone replacement
support.text: Some immune effects need steroids or lasting hormone replacement. Follow the exact prescription and taper. Carry the relevant alert information, and do not stop or reduce these medicines yourself when anticancer treatment is held or completed.

evidence.title: What the evidence means for your treatment
evidence.intro: Discuss the evidence for your diagnosis, tumour test results and treatment setting.
evidence.population: Completely resected melanoma with lymph-node involvement or metastatic disease; the team confirms the stage III or resected stage IV indication. Uveal melanoma is excluded from this adjuvant pathway.
evidence.interpretation: Evidence in advanced melanoma measures control of existing cancer; adjuvant evidence measures recurrence after surgery. Perioperative evidence concerns treatment around surgery. Ask which study and outcome match your stage and plan. These results cannot predict your individual benefit.
limitations: Individual benefit and risk cannot be predicted from a group average.
Your team explains the evidence that applies to this treatment plan and the uncertainty for you as an individual.

chapters.title: Understanding your diagnosis and treatment goal
chapters.intro: Use these questions with your own pathology report and agreed treatment plan.

items.title: What the diagnosis says
items.text: Record the original melanoma site and pathology findings. Breslow thickness and ulceration describe features of the skin tumour; stage describes its extent. Melanoma arising in the eye or a mucosal surface may need a different pathway.

items.title: BRAF and other tumour tests
items.text: BRAF V600 testing can identify an alternative targeted-treatment option in some melanomas. It is separate from the immunotherapy described here. Ask what your tumour result means for the choices available to you.

items.title: Surgery, radiotherapy and medicine have different roles
items.text: Ask whether medicine is intended to reduce recurrence after complete surgery or control cancer that remains. Add any operation or radiotherapy to the plan with its own purpose, timing and risks.

items.title: Stage and response are different
items.text: Stage describes the extent of disease. Response describes a change in measurable cancer during treatment. After complete removal there may be no visible tumour to measure; follow-up then looks for recurrence and treatment effects.

items.title: A new skin change still needs review
items.text: Report a new or changing mole, a sore that persists, a new lump or an unexplained symptom. A photo or a good response in one area cannot rule out a separate problem.

chapters.title: Your medicines and the overall plan
chapters.intro: Nivolumab helps immune cells act against melanoma. After complete surgery, its aim is to lower the risk of recurrence; this does not guarantee that melanoma will not return.

items.title: The schedule in this setting
items.text: Nivolumab every 4 weeks. Adjuvant treatment continues for up to 12 months, subject to safety review.

items.title: How the treatment works
items.text: Nivolumab blocks the PD-1 checkpoint that restrains T cells. The resulting immune activity may control melanoma but can also inflame normal organs. Side effects may first appear after the final dose.

items.title: The role of earlier or later treatment
items.text: Ask how the medicine fits with previous or planned local treatment. The timing of an operation, radiotherapy and a tablet course should be written in one agreed plan.

items.title: Pauses and stopping
items.text: A safety pause is an active treatment decision. Record which medicine is paused, the reason, the tests or recovery needed and who may authorise restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription or reset the history when a new phase begins.

items.title: Previous permanent-stop decisions
items.text: If your team has permanently stopped nivolumab because of a serious immune reaction, improvement does not automatically make restarting safe. Keep that decision in your treatment record; only your specialist team can review further treatment.

chapters.title: Taking treatment and preparing for visits
chapters.intro: Keep the written medicine plan beside this guide; it records your own dose and dates.

items.title: Taking or receiving the medicine
items.text: Nivolumab is given as 480 mg by IV infusion over 60 minutes OR 1200 mg by subcutaneous injection over 3–5 minutes, on Day 1 every 4 weeks. items.text: If a visit is missed or treatment is held, contact the unit for a new plan. Do not count a missed appointment as a dose received. An interval change, operation or new phase does not erase earlier immune toxicity or a permanent-stop decision.

items.title: Other medicines and supplements
items.text: Show the pharmacist a current list of prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, herbal products and supplements. Include anticoagulants, heart medicines, steroids and recent antibiotics. Check before adding, stopping or changing anything; an apparently harmless product can alter treatment or confuse a symptom assessment.

items.title: Practical preparation
items.text: Bring your medicine list, allergy information and questions. Tell the team about practical problems with travel, swallowing, wound care or remembering doses before treatment starts.

chapters.title: Tests: what is required and what each result means
chapters.intro: Safety tests, tumour tests and response scans answer different questions.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: Blood count, kidney and liver tests, glucose and thyroid tests; review autoimmune conditions, transplants, previous immune reactions and all current medicines. BRAF tumour status is checked for the advanced or adjuvant melanoma indication.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Blood count, kidney/liver tests and glucose before every 4-week cycle. Thyroid function is checked before each cycle and when clinically indicated. Cortisol and other tests are added when clinically indicated. Report new symptoms at every visit and between visits; normal blood results do not rule out immune toxicity.

items.title: Scans and tumour markers
items.text: Ask the team to write the next assessment and who will arrange it. Bloods used to monitor kidneys, liver, hormones or muscle are not automatically measures of cancer response. There is no universal tumour-marker blood schedule for these skin-cancer regimens; a scan or extra blood test is requested for a specific clinical reason.

items.title: After a pause or finish
items.text: Continue immune-toxicity monitoring for at least five months after the last dose, and longer when advised. Keep any prescribed steroid taper, hormone replacement and specialist follow-up. Scans follow your individual disease plan.

items.title: Getting the result
items.text: Keep a named contact for bookings and results. If an expected appointment or result is missing, call that service; do not take silence as confirmation that everything is complete.

chapters.title: What to expect between visits
chapters.intro: You can feel well and still need the planned checks. New symptoms deserve attention even on a day without an appointment.

items.title: Your usual pattern
items.text: Record the start and change in symptoms, temperature if advised, bowel pattern, drinking, urine and the effect on normal tasks. A simple few-line record is enough. Use it to describe a change rather than trying to grade or diagnose a toxicity yourself.

items.title: When to call
items.text: Immunotherapy can cause inflammation in healthy organs during treatment or after it stops. Contact the oncology team promptly for new diarrhoea, blood in stools, cough or breathlessness, yellow skin or eyes, severe headache, vision changes, marked thirst, unusual weakness or a spreading rash. Tell any clinician that you are receiving or have received immunotherapy.

items.title: Eating, drinking and activity
items.text: Report nausea, mouth discomfort, diarrhoea or weight loss before they make eating and drinking difficult. The team can adjust symptom support and arrange dietitian or rehabilitation advice.

items.title: A held dose or changed plan
items.text: If a visit is missed or treatment is held, contact the unit for a new plan. Do not count a missed appointment as a dose received. An interval change, operation or new phase does not erase earlier immune toxicity or a permanent-stop decision.

chapters.title: Skin checks, sun protection and optional photographs
chapters.intro: This complements clinical assessment and does not replace it.

items.title: Protect your skin
items.text: Protect exposed skin with clothing, a hat and shade. Use broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and reapply as directed. Avoid sunbeds. Cloudy weather does not remove ultraviolet exposure.

items.title: Know the pattern of your skin
items.text: Ask the team to show you how to check your skin and treated area. Use a mirror or a helper for areas you cannot see. Report a new lump, a changing lesion or a sore that does not heal.

items.title: Photographs are optional
items.text: A private, dated photograph can help describe a change if your team finds it useful. Keep the lighting and size reference consistent. Photographs support a discussion; they do not replace examination and need not be uploaded.

items.title: Wounds, nails and sensitive skin
items.text: Follow the wound and skin-care instructions for the treated area. Ask before adding a cream or remedy. Increasing redness, discharge, pain, bleeding or difficulty using the area needs assessment.

chapters.title: Pregnancy, fertility and protecting others
chapters.intro: Discuss these precautions before treatment even if pregnancy is not currently planned.

items.title: Medicine-specific precautions
items.text: Discuss fertility before starting. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 5 months after the last dose. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy. Discuss breastfeeding restrictions with the team before treatment; do not breastfeed without their advice. Do not stop prescribed steroids or hormone replacement yourself.

items.title: Planning ahead
items.text: Ask early about fertility preservation, sexual health and symptoms affecting intimacy. Tell the team about any chance of pregnancy, breastfeeding or a partner’s pregnancy so that the correct medicine-specific advice can be given. Keep the precautions and their end dates in the written plan.

items.title: Safe handling and supply
items.text: Do not share anticancer medicines. Keep oral medicines in their original labelled packaging, away from children and anyone who could take them accidentally. Return unused medicines to the supplying pharmacy and follow its handling advice. A treatment hold does not remove pregnancy precautions.

chapters.title: Questions, decisions and practical support
chapters.intro: Your priorities and the burden of treatment belong in the discussion.

items.title: Benefits and uncertainties
items.text: Ask what outcome this treatment aims to improve for your diagnosis and what alternatives exist. Results from a study group help a discussion but cannot promise your own result.

items.title: Alternatives and review points
items.text: Agree the next decision point and what would make the plan change. Ask about other suitable treatments, trials and symptom care. Support for comfort and function can continue alongside cancer treatment.

items.title: Help with daily life
items.text: Tell the team what is hardest in daily life: travel, work, caring duties, costs, sleep or confidence. Ask who can help and how to contact them.

items.title: Shared understanding
items.text: Before going home, check that you can describe your medicine schedule, next tests and urgent-contact route. Ask for an interpreter, larger print or a supporter if that would help.

chapters.title: Follow-up and your continuing record
chapters.intro: Keep this record when treatment is paused, changed or completed.

items.title: Your follow-up plan
items.text: Your stage, symptoms and treatment determine follow-up. Write down the skin and lymph-node checks, any body or brain scans and the service arranging them. Confirm your own dates with the team.

items.title: Continuing medicine precautions
items.text: Continue immune-toxicity monitoring for at least five months after the last dose, and longer when advised. Keep any prescribed steroid taper, hormone replacement and specialist follow-up. Scans follow your individual disease plan.

items.title: Treatment summary for other clinicians
items.text: Record the medicines and last dates, important reactions, any long-term hormone replacement or steroid taper, and the responsible oncology contact. Show this information in urgent care and to other specialists. A different treatment phase does not erase earlier toxicity.

items.title: The complete paper version
items.text: Use this handbook as your paper record. Keep the current schedule, medicines, tests and contacts together, and replace outdated pages after a change. The matching QR link is optional.
